item.title: CNMI gubernatorial, AG races still undecided
item.description: No winners have been declared in the 2026 CNMI runoff election as approximately 1,350 absentee ballots remain to be counted. According to updated unofficial results released Saturday by the Commonwealth Election Commission, the Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. leads the race with 6,352 votes, or 53.1% of ballots cast.
item.content:encoded:
No winners have been declared in the 2026 CNMI runoff election as approximately 1,350 absentee ballots remain to be counted.

According to updated unofficial results released Saturday by the Commonwealth Election Commission, the Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. leads the race with 6,352 votes, or 53.1% of ballots cast.

The independent team of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez follows with 5,609 votes, or 46.9%.

In the attorney general race, Joaquin "Jack" DLG Torres has taken a narrow lead with 5,917 votes, or 50.3%, compared to 5,845 votes, or 49.7%, for Michael Evangelista.

The latest figures include ballots from Tinian, which were delayed Friday night due to rough seas and a high surf advisory that prevented election workers from transporting ballots to Saipan.

Before the Tinian votes were added to the tally, Evangelista held a 306-vote advantage over Torres. The additional ballots reversed that outcome and gave Torres a slim 72-vote lead.

Despite the updated count, the results remain unofficial until absentee ballots are canvassed and tabulated. Election officials expect that process to continue through Dec. 4.

The runoff was required after no gubernatorial and AG candidates received more than 50% of the vote in the Nov. 3 general election. Ralph Torres and Jones led that contest with 49.5% of the vote, while Attao and Villagomez finished second with 38.7%, advancing both tickets to the runoff.

While Joaquin Torres led in the Nov. 3 general election with 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, followed by Evangelista with 3,854 votes, or 30.2%.

item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs
item.description: Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented. item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
item.description: GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots." After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
item.content:encoded:
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.

Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.

A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."

There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.

Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

item.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial. Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

item.title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
item.description: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude. It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
item.content:encoded:
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.

It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.

"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.

He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.

"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.

The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."

Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.

In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."

Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

item.content:encoded:
There isn't much to see in Amboy, Calif. But if you're traveling on Route 66, the dusty stop in the Mojave desert is a must for its famous 50-foot-tall neon Roy's Motel and Cafe sign . Photographing the sign can wait: Alan Jacob gets out of his rented GMC truck and heads straight for the gift shop.

Others in Jacob's tour group driving the length of Route 66 have bought T-shirts, hats and socks along the way. One even got a Route 66 tattoo. For the sinewy, retired plumber from a small town about an hour North of New Zealand's capital, Wellington, it's all about the fridge magnets along the nearly month-long journey.

"I've been buying magnets everywhere I go," Jacob said. "When I get home, I'm going to get an 8-by-4 sheet, powder-coat it white, put the road on it and put all the magnets where I got them from."

100 years after its founding , the nearly 2,500-mile highway from Chicago to Santa Monica, Calif., continues to capture imaginations far beyond U.S. borders.

According to a 2024 study conducted by the tourism research firm SMARInsights shared with NPR by the New Mexico Tourism Department, international travelers are more likely to travel the entire length of Route 66 than those from within the United States.

"60 to 70% of the people who come here are international travelers," said Samir Patel, the manager of The Wigwam Motel , a popular stop on the highway in San Bernardino, Calif. "And a good chunk of them are Australians and New Zealanders." The highway has been popular for decades with Europeans, he added, and, in more recent years, with South American and Asian tourists.

Sam Murray, the New Zealand-based owner of Gilligans Tours — loosely named after the 1960s American TV show Gilligan's Island – has been leading Route 66 trips in the spring and fall for more than a decade. His clientele are mostly tourists from New Zealand and Australia.

Murray said he was drawn to Route 66 through his passion for car racing. The 48-year-old first came to the U.S. as an adult in 2005 for an auto race in Laughlin, Nev. When the event was done, Murray drove down a nearby part of Route 66 for the first time. It made him want to do the whole thing.

"So in 2011, I bought an old motor home in Pennsylvania, drove down to St. Louis, followed Route 66 back to LA," he said. "And then I realized when I got home, people that I talked to had an interest as well in doing Route 66."

Of course, "doing Route 66" these days isn't what it once was. The construction of the modern interstate highway system made older sections of the road obsolete. It was officially removed from the system in 1985. Route 66 now exists as an incomplete patchwork of roads, some of them unpaved.

"We've done quite a bit of gravel driving, which is something I didn't expect to do over here," said retired apple grower Pete Volkers. He opted to ride with Murray rather than drive himself in a rented car.

Volkers was looking to venture out on his own for the first time since losing his wife last year to breast cancer, and Route 66 had long been on his bucket list.

He was steeped in mid-20th century American pop culture growing up in New Zealand — "The American diner thing and TV shows like Happy Days, " he recalled.

"On this trip, we've been to so many little towns which have all this stuff that we've seen on TV, and all of these iconic neon signs," said Volkers. "And you just don't get a chance to see that anywhere else in the world."

Volkers said he enjoys wide open roads sprinkled with opportunities to revel in American kitsch and nostalgia. ("At least I can go home and say I slept in a teepee," he said after spending a night in a concrete, teepee-shaped guestroom at the Wigwam Motel.) But Volkers also acknowledges there's a certain bleakness to traveling Route 66 in 2026.

"These little towns that not a lot of people come through. No one stops there," Volkers said. "They're just zooming on to the next big place."

Even if Route 66 isn't what it once was, many stops along the way look like they are thriving — at least for tourists. Oatman, Ariz., is among them.

The windswept former gold mining town is packed with people on a Monday afternoon. To Australian insurance broker Peter Johnson, the rickety clapboard storefronts and local population of roaming donkeys bring classic Westerns to mind. "You should be walking along here with a six gun," Johnson said.

Inside the Oatman Hotel on Main Street, Carrie Eagan is packing bottles of ketchup and mayo instead of a Colt revolver. The restaurant manager at the bustling Route 66 landmark, built in 1902, said she's noticed one main difference between foreign visitors and American ones: "The Americans, they know a lot about the history. But the foreigners are very excited," Eagan said. "They come dressed to impress; ready to go."

This is certainly true of tour participants Kieron and Wendy Guinness. He's sporting a handlebar mustache and white cowboy hat; she's petite and put together in a scarlet sweater. The New Zealand couple are wowed by the thick wads of greenbacks plastering every inch of ceiling and wall space in the Oatman Hotel. "This hotel would be worth a fortune!" Wendy said.

She's been a fan of the United States ever since she spent a year in California as a high school student. "I put on 20 pounds that year because especially when you're young, you come and you're like, 'Oh my God, there's so much good food,'" said Guinness, who managed a women's clothing store before retiring. "We ate out all the time."

Kieron Guinness is nuts about American cars, like many in the group. "I've been around hot rodding all my life, mucking around with old V8s, Chevrolets and Fords and Dodges," he said.

The wiry retired bartender said he has a side hustle importing U.S. cars into New Zealand — despite the fact that steering wheels on American cars are on the left hand side. "And our country's a right-hand drive country," Guinness said.

Waiting in line near the famous " The End of Trail " sign in Santa Monica for a final group photograph, Sam Murray was relieved about making it to the end of Route 66 with no major mishaps.

The tour operator said arriving at the final destination is usually a relief for his guests, too.

"It's not easy," Murray said. "Driving a two-lane highway from downtown Chicago to here is a big expectation for anyone — let alone somebody that's from a country where you drive on the other side of the road."

item.description: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
